title: Zamzam, again
hook: pilgrims drink Zamzam, for whatever purpose it is drunk (Ibn Majah)

segments.voice: Yesterday, two rak'ahs behind Ibrahim's station, and your line: where ibrahim stood. Did you stop for a minute between one thing and the next? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-eight.

A glass of water, and a question before you drink it: what is this for? On an ordinary day, the question doesn't come up. Thirst, habit, the meeting's running long. But there's a hadith in the collection of Ibn Majah that makes the question matter. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is reported to have said that the water of Zamzam is for whatever it is drunk for. Not just for thirst. For whatever the drinker brings to it. We've met this well before on the path. Today it comes back, in the middle of the pilgrimage, with a new job.
screen: `A GLASS OF WATER.` → `WHAT IS THIS FOR?` → `FOR WHATEVER IT IS DRUNK FOR.`

segments.voice: First, where the water comes from. Zamzam is a well inside the sacred mosque in Mecca, close to the Ka'ba. In a long report in Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibn Abbas tells how it first appeared: a mother alone in a dry valley with her baby, searching, and water breaking out of the ground. Her search is tomorrow's story, so for today, just the water. Second, the Prophet at the well. Jabir's account of the pilgrimage, in Sahih Muslim, has him coming to the people of his own clan who were drawing water at Zamzam and giving it out. They handed him a bucket, and he drank. Ibn Abbas adds, in Bukhari, that he was the one who gave the Prophet Zamzam, and that the Prophet drank it standing. A simple scene: a man, a bucket, a crowd, a drink. Third, the hadith from Ibn Majah. Water for whatever it's drunk for. Some pilgrims take that literally. They stand by the taps and fountains and drink, and before they drink, or while they drink, they ask for something. Healing for someone at home. Knowledge. Forgiveness. A child. Some carry bottles of it home for the people who couldn't come. Fourth, what changes. Nothing about the glass is different. The water is still water. What changes is that the drinker stops, names a purpose, and turns a reflex into a request. Scholars have discussed the grading of this hadith, and readers take it in different ways; the habit it has formed is easy to see at the fountains. A drink, and an intention said before it. That's the whole practice.
screen: `A WELL NEAR THE KA'BA.` · `A BUCKET, AND HE DRANK.` · `FOR WHATEVER IT IS DRUNK FOR.` · `A REFLEX TURNED INTO A REQUEST.`

segments.voice: The practice: drink water with an intention. Get a glass of ordinary water, if you can, and hold it. Before you drink, settle, and breathe. Then name one thing you want, for yourself or for someone else, plainly and quietly. If you pray, you can make it a du'a, a request to God in your own words, and say bismillah before you drink. If you don't, just name the hope. Then drink slowly, and sit with the glass. The bell holds the time.
Zamzam. The well beside the Ka'ba, whose water, the hadith says, is for whatever it is drunk for. Today's word.
Your line: drink with intention. Today, before one glass of water, pause and name what it's for. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Pilgrims drink Zamzam water in the sacred mosque, often making a du'a before drinking, and some bring containers of it home to share with family and friends.

notes: Ibn Majah 3062 ('the water of Zamzam is for whatever it is drunk for'): confirm number; its grading is discussed by hadith scholars, and the script says so without naming a grade.
Bukhari 3364 (Ibn Abbas: Hajar, the baby and the water appearing): kept brief, since sa'y is tomorrow; confirm number.
Sahih Muslim 1218 (Jabir: the Prophet came to Banu Abd al-Muttalib drawing Zamzam, they gave him a bucket and he drank): confirm.
Bukhari 1637 (Ibn Abbas: 'I gave the Prophet Zamzam and he drank standing'): confirm number.
'Some carry bottles of it home' is general color; check or soften.
Earlier days on this path covered Zamzam (hence 'again'); the angle here is the Ibn Majah hadith and intention.
